Publisher records online publication 18 March 2024. This supplied file contains the main article, not the separately linked supplementary materials.
source.verification_method: All 18 main-article pages read, including every footnote/reference, Table 1 and Figures 1–6. Figure labels/captions inspected visually. Main identity checked with Cambridge; narrow publisher/Crossref bibliography checks and Bansak identification passages surfaced in publisher-indexed search results do not constitute full reading of the cited books/methods papers. citation.title: The Paradox of Algorithms and Blame on Public Decision-makers

reading.source_scope_note: Two vignette experiments on three U.S. public samples examine observer blame when a judge grants probation and a released repeat drunk driver later kills a pedestrian. Study 1 pools Lucid 923 attention-check passers and 1,842 TESS respondents; Study 2 reports 1,423 passers. Advice agreement changes the recommendation as well as conformity. Secondary conceptual labels and post-treatment perception measures are distinguished from observed judge conduct, causal mediators and actual democratic accountability.
access_limits: Separate SI.1–SI.16, complete vignettes/items, exact model tables, registration records, respondent comments and mediation-sensitivity outputs were not independently read.

Study 1 discloses initial Lucid collection before registration but analysis afterwards. The author account is recorded; chronology and prespecification were not independently verified. The Dataverse link remains a publication placeholder in the supplied text.
No original cited book, actual judge, current law, independent raw analysis or intervention on a mediator was examined.

study.samples: Study 1: June 2021 Lucid collection of 1,500, 923 passing attention checks (61.5%); TESS/AmeriSpeak 1,842 received four months after the stated 22 June 2021 registration, pooled with Lucid. No further TESS flow is supplied in the main article. Study 2: March 2022 Lucid, 3,656 entering and 1,423 passing (38.9%, described as 40%), against an overview target of about 1,400. These reported analysis counts sum to 4,188 participations; cross-panel uniqueness, weighting and retained-sample representativeness are not verified.
study.design: Study 1 has seven between-person conditions: unaided judge; AI, experienced probation officer or joint advice, each agreeing with probation or recommending imprisonment that the judge rejects. Every judge grants probation; every released repeat drunk driver then kills a pedestrian. Thus agreement versus disagreement changes substantive advice and evidential warning as well as conformity. Source labels also describe distinct expertise, and joint advice adds a second source.
study.study2: Three conditions retain unaided, agreeing with AI and disagreeing with AI. Outcomes add a seven-expert trust/distrust index; retrospective expected accuracy; and perceived versus desired locus of judgment (judge versus advice source). Full item wording, scoring and timing beyond the described post-treatment measures require the unread supplement.
study.outcomes: Blame of the judge and available advice sources on 1–10 scales, rescaled 0–1. Scores are independent endorsements, not shares summing to a fixed budget. Respondents judge hypothetical actors; no judge chooses reliance, deploys an algorithm, imposes punishment or changes actual sentencing behavior.
study.study1_results: Relative to the unaided control, algorithm agreement increases judge blame by about .09 and disagreement by about .06 on the 0–1 scale; Figure 1 treatments range about .053–.09. These are fractions of the full response scale, not 9%/6% relative changes or probabilities. Reported d=.16–.28. Pairwise advice-source and agreement/disagreement differences are not significant (p>.10); this is not equivalence. Blame of advice sources can coexist with blame of the judge rather than displacing it.
study.moderation1: No reported demographic moderation for age, gender, race or education. More Republican identification has positive ATMEs for AI agreement .04 [.02,.06], AI disagreement .03 [.01,.05], and joint disagreement .03 [.01,.05]. AI-trust moderation for agreement −.110 [−.23,.004] includes zero; disagreement −.025 [−.14,.09] also does. The printed joint-agreement estimate .03 with interval [−.09,.05] is not a centered symmetric Wald interval as described; original output is needed before changing values.
study.models: OLS treatment contrasts, 1,000 coefficient draws for uncertainty. Moderation uses parallel within-treatment regressions and differences in moderator slopes. Treatment randomization alone does not remove confounding of a nonrandom moderator; causal moderation requires additional identification assumptions. Individual within-arm significance is not a direct between-arm contrast.
study.study2_results: Figure 3 shows positive total contrasts of roughly .02–.03 with 95% intervals crossing zero; the source reports p>.05, and no agreement/disagreement difference p>.10. This does not prove exact no effect or rule out context-specific protection. No clinical, electoral, contractual or incarceration outcome is evaluated by these main blame ratings.
study.expert_trust: When the judge rejects AI advice, trust in experts is positively related to blame (within-arm p<.001), and the displayed ATME excludes zero. Agreement moderation is negative but uncertain. Prose says high-versus-low trust means about 33% greater blame under disagreement and 17% lower under agreement; these within-arm descriptions are not identical to the difference-in-slopes ATME. The seven-expert index and covariate sufficiency are not independently validated.
study.accuracy_expectations: Higher retrospective expected accuracy relates to higher blame in both conditions. Agreement does not significantly raise expectations; disagreement lowers them. These results do not support a simple positive mediation chain from advice through heightened expectations to extra blame. The same vignette outcome is always known, so outcome/hindsight bias itself is not isolated.
study.abdication_mediation: Agreement shifts desired locus toward the judge (path .897); desired judge judgment relates to blame (.019); product ≈.017. Figure 6 reports indirect .017, 95% bootstrap [.007,.030], p<.001 and proportion .660, with displayed total .026 (p=.210). Lack of a significant total does not preclude an indirect effect, but a ratio to a small uncertain total can be unstable. Mediator is post-treatment and not randomized; the authors explicitly disclose confounding concerns and sample-specific lack of robustness. Do not call 66% a securely identified psychological explanation.
study.reporting: Figure 4 caption names panels 5a–d although its own panels are 4a–d. Figure 5 caption names 3a–d instead of 5a–d. Figure 6a caption describes disagreement moderation, but actual panel 6a is the agreement→desired-judgment path; 6b is judgment→blame, 6c the path diagram. Page 212 text mentions 6d although Figure 6 has only a–c. The diagram prints AMCE while context defines ACME. These are directly inspectable locator/label problems, not grounds to fabricate numerical corrections.
study.limits_of_inference: The study holds the adverse outcome fixed, tests public blame rather than elite strategy and acknowledges advice/control wording differences. It cannot establish that no accountability gap exists, that all ethical concerns are refuted, that XAI/impact assessments repair blame, or that unnecessary detention and release errors are evaluated the same. Retrospective Type S/M calculations are assumption-dependent conditional diagnostics, not posterior probabilities that the substantive theory is false.

summary: Add math washing as a conceptual presentation practice and perceived abdication of responsibility as an observer appraisal, with explicit evidence limits. Enrich existing blame, scapegoating, authority and epistemic-trust entries. The experiment does not show reliable blame shielding, but source nulls are not equivalence or proof that democratic accountability is secure. Preserve disclosed mediation fragility, scale units and nonrandom-moderator assumptions; correct reliable book-author roles, article-year/volume metadata and figure locators.

findings.definition: Presenting a contestable judgment as objective or beyond challenge because it is expressed through numbers or an algorithm.
findings.origin: AI ethics / social evaluation of quantitative authority
findings.novelty_rationale: Algorithmic authority describes treating an algorithm as credible. Math washing describes a presentation practice that obscures contestable assumptions behind an appearance of mathematical objectivity; the receiver’s trust and the communicator’s justification are distinct. No named washing entry exists.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Conceptual secondary label discussed in the read article; its experiments do not directly manipulate or establish successful objectivity washing. Original cited books and essays were not independently read.
findings.ai_proposal: Present the same recommendation with equivalent uncertainty and assumptions either exposed or hidden behind quantitative language, then assess whether users misjudge evidential support and whether a model uses numbers to evade a requested justification. Hold predictive information and actual performance fixed.

evidence.quote:
base their decisions on “more
objective” criteria and/or a way for avoiding responsibility for difficult, discretionary decisions.

findings.evidence_scope: The introduction reports a critique that numerical/algorithmic framing can lend contested decisions an appearance of objectivity and responsibility cover. This is a secondary conceptual definition; judge-blame experiments do not test the mathematical presentation itself or demonstrate successful washing. Shane (2019) and the other originals were cited, not fully read.
findings.boundary: Using mathematics, valid evidence or an appropriate algorithm is not itself washing. Show that quantitative presentation conceals contestability or overstates justification. The study’s lack of blame shielding neither proves washing impossible nor licenses a claim that all quantitative decisions manipulate people.

findings.definition: Judging that a person has failed to exercise the independent judgment expected of their role by relying on another source.
findings.novelty_rationale: This is an observer’s role-duty appraisal. Displacement of responsibility instead concerns the actor’s reduced felt responsibility; blame is the resulting fault judgment, not the same perception. No existing entry names this observer appraisal.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human observer perception measured after a hypothetical judicial decision; proposed model behavior and objectively unjustified delegation were not directly demonstrated.
findings.ai_proposal: Vary whether an AI-supported decision maker independently checks relevant evidence and gives task-specific reasons, holding outcome and recommendation fixed. Measure perceived abandonment of role duties separately from blame and actual oversight quality; test a model’s own verification/provenance under an explicit responsibility contract.

findings.evidence_scope: Study 2 asks whose evaluation the decision reflected and whose evaluation should dominate. Agreement with AI relates to greater desired use of the judge’s own judgment and a positive statistical indirect association with blame. Post-treatment measurement and explicitly nonrobust mediation limit any claim that this appraisal causally produces blame.
findings.boundary: A perception is not proof of abandoned duty; appropriate authorized delegation can preserve responsibility. Independent judgment does not mean rejecting correct advice. This differs from deliberate scapegoating, the actor’s felt displacement, actual control and the amount of assigned blame.

findings.evidence_scope: Three U.S. samples judge an adverse probation decision. In pooled Study 1, agreeing or disagreeing with AI each raises judge blame slightly relative to unaided control; Study 2 contrasts remain positive but uncertain. Source-condition differences are not significant, and assigning blame to advice sources need not reduce judge blame.
findings.boundary: These are independent hypothetical ratings, not a fixed blame budget or demonstrated actual liability. Null contrasts do not prove equivalence, and fixed negative outcomes do not isolate outcome bias. Advice content and agreement differ together.

findings.definition: Deflecting personal or collective responsibility for a negative outcome by directing blame toward another person, group or entity.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain the existing concept and add this judicial-context evidence/boundary rather than an overlapping row.

findings.evidence_scope: Boundary only: the paper tests whether public blame ratings offer cover for a hypothetical judge’s adoption of algorithm advice. It finds no consistent reduction, while policy evasion incentives remain theoretical. No judge deliberately chooses automation to escape responsibility.
findings.boundary: An absence of reliable blame shielding in this vignette does not establish no scapegoating anywhere. Fault endorsement by an observer, strategic deflection by an actor and real institutional sanctions differ.

findings.definition: Treating an algorithmic system as a credible or legitimate source for deciding what information to accept or how to act.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain the existing concept and add this judicial-context evidence/boundary rather than an overlapping row.

findings.evidence_scope: Boundary only: algorithms are discussed as purportedly objective expert advice, but AI/human/joint source differences in judge blame are not significant. This outcome does not directly measure acceptance of advice, perceived objectivity or legitimacy.
findings.boundary: Do not infer algorithmic authority from a number appearing in a vignette, or infer its universal absence from observer blame. Math washing is the presentation practice; authority is the source’s perceived standing.

findings.definition: Relying on another as a source of knowledge because of perceived competence, experience or reasoning ability.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain the existing concept and add this judicial-context evidence/boundary rather than an overlapping row.

findings.evidence_scope: A seven-expert trust/distrust index moderates blame in the AI-disagreement condition: greater reported expert trust corresponds to more judge blame for rejection. This concerns a human observer’s attitude toward expertise, not a model’s personal trust or proof that the recommendation was objectively warranted.
findings.boundary: Randomizing advice conditions does not randomize the trust index. Causal moderator claims require assumptions beyond parallel regressions; within-arm slopes and between-arm moderation are different. Appropriate skepticism need not be anti-intellectualism.

methodological_limits: Only a hypothetical probation release followed by a pedestrian death is tested. Agreement, advice content and warning severity covary. Public judgments cannot stand in for actual judge reliance incentives, legal liability or democratic accountability.

Attention-check exclusions are substantial and may alter representativeness. Initial Lucid data precede registration by disclosure; data inspection chronology and retained panel composition are not independently verified. Cross-sample pooled null differences are not equivalence.
Advice-source blame and judge blame are separately rated, not conserved. Similar source conditions do not prove no attribution mechanism or an absence of algorithm-specific effects in other tasks.

Randomized treatment does not randomize expert trust or post-treatment judgment perceptions. Parallel moderation and mediation require additional assumptions, overlap and sensitivity checks. The authors themselves acknowledge sample-specific nonrobust mediation.

The 66% proportion is a ratio with a small uncertain total; it is not a precise population share. A nonsignificant total is compatible with an indirect association, so do not reject mediation solely on that basis.

No successful-outcome/no-outcome contrast isolates outcome bias or hindsight bias. Expected accuracy after the event may reflect an appropriate normative judgment or reconstruction, not necessarily a cognitive error.

Scale fractions, relative percentage increases, within-arm slopes and treatment-moderation contrasts are different quantities. Conditional sign/magnitude diagnostics do not prove universal absence or exact zero probability of an opposite substantive effect.

The unread supplement contains exact coefficients, weights, checks and sensitivity analyses. Label/locator errors can be corrected confidently; uncertain CIs, p values and data flow must not be repaired by guessing.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Awad’s car-control vignette gives both shared-control actors intervention opportunities. The present judge retains decision authority. Higher human blame is not itself a crumple zone; different task roles and independent ratings should remain distinct.

Dawtry’s robot/machine label changes target blame without consistently exonerating human managers. This judicial experiment likewise shows that blaming an algorithm need not subtract blame from a human; endorsement ratings are not a fixed responsibility budget.

The national-security study measures actual answer revision by public respondents, whereas this study measures observer blame of a fictional decision maker. Neither aggregate switching nor observer blame alone establishes real institutional accountability or a policymaker’s evasion motive.

deferred.reason: These are predicted directional contrasts in an attribution experiment, not newly demonstrated independent mechanisms. Existing blame attribution, scapegoating and responsibility concepts retain the contextual results.

Brief secondary labels span technological framing and legitimation and are not automatically synonyms. This review defines the specific math-washing presentation practice only; the original books/essays were not read, so broader labels need their own source review.

The study uses a general expert-trust index, not an independently isolated prejudice mechanism or a full definition review of anti-intellectualism. Enrich existing epistemic-trust boundaries; do not equate justified skepticism with bias.

Existing concepts; all participants know the same adverse outcome, so the paper’s retrospective-bias interpretation does not isolate either effect. No additional row or evidential credit for those mechanisms.

limitations: All 18 supplied pages were read; separate SI, registration and raw outputs were not. Counts and quotations refer to the supplied version.
Narrow primary bibliographic and methodological checks do not imply full reading of the referenced books, Bansak paper, court record or contemporary legislation.

interpretation_qualifications.qualification: Parallel regressions do not automatically confer causal moderation. Bansak’s identification section requires assumptions about the nonrandom moderator, including conditional independence/common support; treatment randomization alone is insufficient. This does not prove the authors’ estimates invalid, but their causal interpretation requires the unavailable covariate/assumption assessment.
interpretation_qualifications.verification_scope: Narrow check of identification passages surfaced in publisher-indexed search results and the abstract. Direct full-page access redirected and failed; the entire section/paper was not independently read. No independent behavior-paper credit.

interpretation_qualifications.qualification: A .09 contrast on the normalized 0–1 blame scale is 9% of the full response scale, not necessarily a 9% relative increase in blame. The article itself defines the scale fraction; retain that interpretation.

Nonzero indirect association with an uncertain total is statistically possible. The .660 mediated proportion is not securely identified causal explanatory power; confounding and weak robustness are explicitly disclosed.

The abstract loosely says respondents assign more blame when they disagree with the algorithm. The body separates a positive trust-related moderation from an average treatment contrast that crosses zero; keep the conditional and average findings distinct.
